#3432. ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!” Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

To be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go big or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

If that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

The bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

It’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.)

If there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

On paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

#3431. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3429. GTA 6: Easiest Ways To Earn Money

As in many open-world games, cash rules everything in GTA 6. You need it to properly prep for some of the tougher encounters in the game, and there are so many ways to earn money that it can be overwhelming. It is an open-world, expansive adventure, after all, but there are plenty of ways to simplify making money.

In addition to robbing places with Jason and Lucia together, you can string multiple robberies into one long crime session, or opt for more legitimate ways to earn money. No matter which option you choose, here are the easiest ways to earn cash in GTA 6.

It sounds obvious, but mainlining story missions is an easy way to earn cash and advance the campaign. Early on, Jason will get constant payments from jobs in his mailbox, so check it nearly every morning before driving off the property.

Some story missions can offer incredibly luxurious rewards, like gear, clothes, weapons, and of course, tons of cash. Some mid-to-late game missions offer tens of thousands of dollars in rewards, quickly boosting your bank account without doing much beyond playing the story.

Once you get to Chapter 2 with Lucia and meet Moses, you'll have the power to bring him cars, and either "register" them (so you own them above board), or sell them.

All you need to do is get in the car, then drive it to Moses (marked clearly on the map in the northwest portion of the game world), drive it into his garage, interact with him (L2/LT) and manually sell or register the car.

Selling nicer cars to Moses is a very easy way to get a ton of cash early in the game, and beyond.

Very early in GTA 6, you can knock off convenience stores and pawn shops, most of which have either one armored guard (who can easily be taken out as you enter) or no protection at all.

Walk into the store, take out the armed NPCs, and then point a gun at an employee. Hold L2 (LT) to bring up a prompt (typically confirmed with Square on PlayStation, X on Xbox), asking them to take money out of the cash register or let you know where valuables are kept.

Depending on where you rob, there might be an additional opportunity for extra cash:

Once you have the illegal goods (which are typically substances or marked bills), you'll need to deliver them to a specific NPC (marked in green on the world map) to "clean" them. This includes marked bills from banks, or illegal substances seized from enemy operations. Just bring the items (housed in a duffel bag) to the NPC, speak to them, and hand them over with a button prompt.

If you die or get caught by the police in GTA 6, you'll lose your goods in the duffel bag, so keep that in mind. If you're doing a huge job and have tons of cash and illegal goods in a duffel bag, you'll want to turn it in to a helpful NPC sooner rather than later.

#3428. Ridley Scott's Sci-Fi Masterpiece Could Return to Theaters in a Shocking Way, Producers Reveal

The producers of Blade Runner 2099 want to carefully expand the franchise

The producers of Blade Runner 2099 want to carefully expand the franchise

Blade Runner, Ridley Scott’s 1982 adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, is one of the best and most influential sci-fi films of all time, but it took 35 years for it to get a direct sequel. Producers Broderick Johnson and Andrew Kosove acquired the rights to the franchise in 2011 through their production company, Alcon, and used them to develop Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049, which is set 30 years after the events of Scott’s film. Now, the timeline is moving forward again in Blade Runner 2099, which premieres on Prime Video on Nov. 25, and the producers are already thinking about what’s next for the cyberpunk series after that.

“We've been very judicious not to overexpose the IP or flood the marketplace, but strategically we're always thinking about the next chapters in the franchise,” Johnson tells Polygon. “This was a long, challenging, but very fulfilling journey that we hope audiences enjoy that really fills out a lot more of the mythology because it's all in canon. We're definitely thinking about new things to do with the next iteration.”

Blade Runner 2099 has been in development since 2021, and was disrupted by the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike and the departure of director and executive producer Jeremy Podeswa. Johnson says managing such a beloved property is “a blessing and a challenge.” Annapurna Interactive announced in 2023 that it was working on a video game adaptation titled Blade Runner 2023: Labyrinth, but that project seems to have been scrapped after most of the team resigned in 2024. The producers have also spoken with game studios about making a AAA game in the style of Cyberpunk 2077.

“People approach us all the time with different ideas,” Johnson said. “There's a very high bar for anything that you do in this universe. But we love that challenge. It's so dear to artists’ and creators' hearts that we're always getting interesting ideas about what to do next.”

The Blade Runner franchise also includes a trio of short films and the 2021 animated series Blade Runner: Black Lotus, which are all set between the events of the two movies. Kosove said they’re now trying to decide what storyline they want to explore for their next project, and what the right medium is.

“We may go backwards in the other direction and explore what happened before the first movie,” he says. “We could continue it in television potentially, and at some point we will certainly go back to film because we believe Blade Runner is fundamentally a theatrical property. But we get inquiries about theater and even opera and other things. We've got a lot of options on our plate and we're exploring them carefully now.”

In Blade Runner 2099, the Replicants have led a successful uprising against humanity. The series follows the human fugitive Cora (Hunter Schafer) as she teams up with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant with only days left to live, to track down Olwen’s former partner and the secrets he’s hiding. Kosove and Johnson previously worked on The Expanse, and Kosove learned a key lesson from the adaptation of James S.A. Corey’s sci-fi series.

“Ultimately in any genre, you have to care about the characters,” he says. “The performances of Hunter and Michelle are amazing. Because it’s television, which is long-form, you can get into character development in a way that’s harder to do in film. We’re really hoping people delve into the characters in a meaningful way.”

Blade Runner 2099 was written as an 8-episode limited series that wraps up its character arcs, though it leaves plenty of room for expansion.

“As a Blade Runner fan, I would always take more Blade Runner,” showrunner Silka Luisa tells Polygon. “What I love about both films was that they didn’t answer all the questions. You’re not walking out of them knowing exactly what’s going to happen afterwards, and it left space for your own imagination to fill in how it could continue. That’s what we tried to do here.”

#3427. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3426. Every Show Premiering on ABC in Winter 2026–2027

September and October mark the end of summer, the return to school, and the premieres of network TV shows, either returning with new seasons or introducing their inaugural ones. But there's also a winter schedule that helps keep the momentum going after the holiday break. Some shows come back at the end of the year or beginning of the new year, through March.

Many popular series that came back during the 2026 fall season return in winter after their midseason holiday breaks. For ABC, this includes shows like Grey's Anatomy, 9-1-1, Abbott Elementary, R.J. Decker, and Scrubs. But there's plenty more to watch, too, with shows debuting their long-awaited new seasons and a couple of brand-new titles to add to your watch list.

Did you even know American Idol is still on the air? Yes, the reality singing competition is still going. Technically, American Idol did end in 2016, but it left a huge hole in the primetime TV lineup and came back in 2018, complete with Ryan Seacrest as host once again. There has been a rotating list of judges, but the latest, Carrie Underwood, Luke Bryan, and Lionel Richie, all return this season.

As usual, you'll see aspiring singers from all walks of life audition in hopes of making their dreams of becoming a star come true. It happened to people like Kelly Clarkson, Chris Daughtry, and Underwood herself, after all. It's the perfect show to watch with the kids or put on when "nothing's on" to enjoy in the background.

One of the most endearing characters in a police procedural of late, quirky accent and all, Will Trent (Ramón Rodríguez) of Will Trent has a special knack for solving cases as a GBI Special Agent in Atlanta. He can look at a crime scene and piece together what happened in his head. It's a byproduct of his traumatic upbringing as an orphan and foster child as well as his dyslexia.

Season 5 of the perfect mystery show picks up in the aftermath of an immense tragedy that rocked Will's friends and co-workers. There will likely be a lot of changes to the dynamic as well as new characters. Alexandra Metz is set to play the new GBI Deputy Director, Birdie Palmer. Fans can't wait to find out what's next for Will and others, like Angie (Erika Christensen), who have suffered tremendous loss.

The return of this crime comedy drama, about a high-intellect single mom who helps the local police force's homicide division solve crimes, is one of the most anticipated of the season given that High Potential has historically premiered in September. It was pushed forward this year to make room for Scrubs and allow the season to flow more nicely instead of going on hiatus through the holidays. But fans are on edge given that Season 2 ended with a massive revelation and cliffhanger.

While the story in one of the best network procedurals on TV right now continues to function as a case-of-the-week procedural, the overarching narrative of what happened to Morgan's (Kaitlin Olson) first husband, Roman, is coming together. And things are getting dangerous, potentially deadly. High Potential's return is so anticipated that ABC is premiering a special episode on February 14, 2027, immediately following the Super Bowl. Airing it outside its regular timeslot, and in such a coveted space, suggests ABC has high hopes that High Potential will return strong.

For lovers of true crime docuseries and news programming, ABC has a new investigative docuseries coming next year that sounds intriguing. Surviving a Scandal explores various situations when a famous (or not-so-famous) figure was marred by controversy that turned their lives and careers upside down. Thanks to the media and especially the tabloids, this can cause massive damage while also potentially revealing secrets and lies.

There's no shortage of news cases to cover for a show like this or individuals to highlight, from actors to musicians, politicians and other public figures. Already, we know a few people who will be covered in this series, including Milli Vanilli, Octomom, and Joey Buttafuoco. The idea is to rehash what happened during the biggest controversies in their lives and look at how these situations impacted their sense of self. I'll be tuning into this one for sure.

The Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

You are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You said what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

The Tim Allen and Kat Dennings sitcom returns for its third season to delight fans with its dark yet fun humor. In Shifting Gears, Matt Parker (Allen) has lost his wife and his estranged and now divorced daughter Riley (Dennings) moves in with her two daughters. None of this sits well with the gruff and surly Matt, but family is family, after all.

With this being its ninth season, The Rookie becomes the third-longest-running ABC series. The police procedural stars Nathan Fillion as John Nolan, a 40-year-old divorcee who decides that part of his new lease on life will involve making a big move from Pennsylvania to Los Angeles and becoming an LAPD officer. Being the oldest rookie on the force has its own challenges, but it's relatable to any industry, too.

Inspired by a true story, The Rookie, one of the best network procedurals, has a loyal following of fans who will undoubtedly be excited to tune in and cozy up every Wednesday night with new episodes. It's all about day-to-day police work, but you're seeing it from the lens of a man who, at times, feels out of place. But most importantly, he's determined to prove he can do this and handle anything the job throws at him, no matter his age.

You get a full two hours of The Rookie with the original series serving as the lead-in to this new spin-off, The Rookie: North. Set in Pierce County, it's a similar story with Alex Holland (Jay Ellis) being in a situation somewhat like John's. Following a violent home invasion, Alex decides that he's going to finally prove to himself and others that he can find purpose by joining the local police department.

The cases and scenery will be different given that the rural forest is not far away. Plus, being in such a secluded area, the officers can't easily call for back-up when something goes awry. We don't yet know much about this show, but Ellis will be joined by Chris Sullivan (This Is Us), Janet Montgomery (New Amsterdam), and Karen Fukuhara (The Boys), all veterans of the small screen.

There's nothing better to flex your brain muscles while relaxing at home on a Friday night than to watch Jeopardy! with the family. Celebrity Jeopardy! makes it even more fun. It's a less serious version of the game for charity with questions that the average person will actually be able to answer. Go ahead and pat yourself on the back for getting some right.

With Mina Kimes having won the latest "All Stars" season after going up against heavyweights Ike Barinholtz and Steven Weber, we still don't know who will be in this season. What we do know is Ken Jennings is back as host, and there will be plenty of money on the table for great charities.

#3425. Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

Ever since George Lazenby first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” fans have argued over who makes the best 007 — and those arguments are likely to resume once Robert Pattinson takes the screen as the latest Bond in director Denis Villeneuve’s new iteration. Although Craig has his partisans, Connery tends to be the consensus choice for the best Bond, though I’ve argued here for the merits of 1970s and ’80s Roger Moore. All the Bonds have their virtues, but Connery benefited from being there first — for anyone who discovered the series in its initial heyday, Connery simply is James Bond. Related Stories ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’? ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Yet Connery actually wasn’t the first actor to play Bond. That honor goes to journeyman MGM contract player Barry Nelson, who played Bond in a “Casino Royale” adaptation eight years before Connery made the character famous in “Dr. No.” Connery may have been the first 007 to grace the big screen, but Nelson established Bond on the small screen in an episode of the CBS anthology series “Climax!” opposite Peter Lorre in the Le Chiffre role that would later be inhabited by Orson Welles (in the goofy 1967 “Casino Royale”) and Mads Mikkelsen (in the 2006 adaptation that introduced Craig to the series).

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is a fascinating artifact that includes elements that would go on to characterize future James Bond movies, while also going in a few other very different directions. The key difference is in the scale, stripped down by necessity for television production. The hour-long “Climax!” episode is all interiors, taking place entirely in the hotel and casino of the title. It’s more a James Bond play than a movie, with Bond and Le Chiffre facing off in a series of verbal — and ultimately physical — jousts in confined spaces, and it’s surprisingly effective.

It’s also a very strange beginning for a franchise that would come to be known for its globetrotting locales and elaborate action set pieces. Not that this “Casino Royale” was officially part of the James Bond franchise as we know it. In fact, although there have been three adaptations of Ian Fleming’s first James Bond novel, only the third incarnation with Daniel Craig was from EON Productions, the company that controlled the character from “Dr. No” through the Craig era before selling the rights to Amazon.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” came about when producer Gregory Ratoff optioned the rights to Fleming’s novel in May of that year. The novel wasn’t yet a hit, and Fleming was sorely in need of cash, which led him to make one of the worst deals in movie-rights history when he sold the book outright to Ratoff for $6,000 after the TV episode aired. This left “Casino Royale” out of the deal when EON secured the screen rights to James Bond as a character, so Bond producers Albert Broccoli and Harry Saltzman could only sit back and grit their teeth when Ratoff turned “Casino Royale” into a comedy in 1967 and cast Peter Sellers, David Niven, Woody Allen and others as rotating Bonds.

EON ultimately made a deal to bring “Casino Royale” under their umbrella and used the novel to reboot the franchise with Craig, but in 1954 it served as the source for a much more modest affair. The biggest similarities between the 1954 “Climax!” episode and the Daniel Craig movie come in the time spent on extended gambling sequences, and the centering of a brutal torture scene. Given censorship restrictions of the time, Nelson’s torture in a bathtub is considerably less graphic than the mallet to the testicles inflicted on Craig, but it’s rough enough stuff for a 1950s TV production.

Certain aspects of Nelson’s characterization, like Bond’s mix of sexual swagger and icy indifference, would later be adopted by most future 007s, to varying degrees. The biggest difference between Nelson and future Bonds is a simple one: He’s American. Although Broccoli and Saltzman flirted with the idea of an American Bond throughout the series’ history (going so far as to cast James Brolin in “Octopussy” before Moore decided to return at the last minute), to date they’ve never actually pulled the trigger on casting outside the UK.

Nelson is probably best known to modern audiences as the affable hotel manager Stuart Ullman in Stanley Kubrick’s “The Shining,” but in the 1950s he was a sturdy character actor and occasional leading man who bounced around television after an initial sojourn as a studio contract player. As a young man, he appeared in several important MGM films, including “Shadow of the Thin Man,” “Bataan,” and “A Guy Named Joe” (the source material for Steven Spielberg’s “Always”). Later on, he popped up in “Airport” and had a successful Broadway career. He was nominated for a Tony acting opposite Liza Minnelli in Martin Scorsese’s 1977 production “The Act.”

In 1954, though, he was in the middle of a prolific and productive era as a TV stalwart, both as a series regular (on “The Hunter” and “My Favorite Husband”) and a frequent guest star. He doesn’t exhibit a ton of range as American “Combined Intelligence” agent “Jimmy” Bond, but that too is in keeping with the overall conception of the character, at least until Craig tried to bring a little more emotional depth to the role.

In Americanizing Bond, the “Climax!” edition of “Casino Royale” ends up making a number of related changes that are small but make the film feel just a bit off for fans of the EON productions. American Felix Leiter (later played by Jeffrey Wright) becomes Brit Clarence Leiter, for example. Although there’s none of the Bond gadgetry that would become famous later, there are hints of what’s to come in the form of props like a villain’s cane that hides a gun, and the opening credits for the “Climax!” series itself feature a gun barrel pointed at the viewer that predicts the iconic graphics of later Bond title sequences.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is noteworthy for another reason: its composer, Jerry Goldsmith, who would ultimately score hundreds of major films, including “Planet of the Apes,” “Chinatown,” “Basic Instinct,” and most of Joe Dante’s work. Yet in some ways what’s fascinating about “Casino Royale” is how unremarkable it is — it’s a decent, solid piece of entertainment from an era when proliferating anthology shows provided similar programs every week.

If Fleming had his way, it would have only been the start for 007 on television; he wrote several outlines for episodes of a James Bond series before CBS canceled the project. Luckily, he repurposed most of what he wrote as short stories for his 1960 book “For Your Eyes Only,” and television’s loss was cinema’s gain. By 1962, James Bond belonged to the movies — and to Sean Connery.

#3424. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3423. GTA 6: How To Get Any Safe Code

GTA 6 is full of surprises. While there are tons of ways to make money, some of them are faster than others. But those methods are generally riskier, creating an interesting push-and-pull in how fast you earn cash in the game.

While other GTA games have had these elements front and center, GTA 6 expands the robbery mechanic quite a bit, allowing players to use disguises and hit a ton of places in rapid succession, quicker than ever before. There are a lot of factors to consider, but here's how to get any safe code, whether it's a small pawn shop or a big bank.

For the most part, there are two core methods for gaining access to the safe code, beyond improbably guessing the combination:

Before you do any of that, turn off the security feed and make sure you're isolated from what's going on outside. Taking Jason or Lucia with you can help you control the crowd, and avoid the police showing up earlier as you're searching for (or demanding) the safe code.

Generally, smaller places (like pawn shops) will have the code written down, and one employee present. These codes might be on a giant board close to the register, in a back room, or in an office.

The easiest way to try and force the code out of an employee. You can hold them up directly by aiming a weapon at them, holding L2 (LT on Xbox), and repeatedly pressing the Square (X on Xbox) button. You'll interrogate them for a code, and even if they don't give it to you, you can still try the same method on someone else. This method may also force NPCs to take cash out of the register and place it on the counter, making your robbery go a little faster.

Often, in the hectic event of robbing something (especially if it's a massive bank), it's easy to miss the notification that you acquired a safe code verbally. Because of this, make sure you look for the safe before leaving a bank for any reason, in case you picked up the safe code by accident. It'll take less than 30 seconds to load up your duffle bag with cash from the safe.

For the most part, any business will have an on-site safe, but that's not always the case. Look for locations to rob with a specific icon that shows how much cash the store has on hand and whether there are any illicit items in the backroom (like illegal substances).

That said, banks are one of the biggest-yield targets in GTA 6, so if you're going to hit one of those, make sure you go for the big rewards:

Robbing a place in GTA 6 with a low yield can get you caught in a nasty, escalating police chase, which can waste time and net you zero rewards if you end up dying or getting caught.

#3422. GTA 6 Really Is Better On PS5 Than Xbox

If you’re planning to get Grand Theft Auto 6 at launch, you’ll be able to buy it on two consoles: PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. But while both are capable pieces of hardware, it sure seems like developer Rockstar Games has a preference between the two. Advertisements for the game have declared that it “plays best on PS5.” Sony has even gotten custom GTA 6 DualSense controllers in celebration of the launch. To some, it could look like GTA 6 is a PS5 exclusive, even though it very much is not.

Now that I’ve finally played GTA 6 for myself, it’s very clear why Sony’s console is the center of attention. It’s not so much about raw power, though the PS5 Pro is likely the best way for the techiest gamers to play, until we get a PC port; it has more to do with the DualSense. GTA 6 feels like it was built with the controller and its unique features in mind, making it a stronger sales pitch for the PS5 than most of Sony’s actual exclusives. It’s just a shame it’s coming so late in the console’s life cycle.

In terms of how GTA 6 runs on PS5, there are no real surprises there. I largely played on PS5 Pro, which was able to give me a relatively smooth 30 frames per second performance. I did experience some framerate dips during high-level police chases, but it otherwise impresses considering the sheer scale of the world and its high level of detail throughout. I’ve yet to test it on Xbox Series X, but there are no red flags here that suggest it might struggle on Microsoft’s console. (The Xbox Series S is a wildcard.)

What was instantly more noticeable during my playthrough was how GTA 6 goes all-in on the DualSense, to the point where it feels like Rockstar built the game specifically around the controller. You can see that in the little details. For instance, Jason and Lucia have cell phones that they can bring up at any time to send texts, make calls, and check apps. The sounds from that phone come through the DualSense’s built-in speaker. If someone calls you, you’ll hear the ring from the controller instead of the TV. That makes it feel like you, the player, are literally holding that phone in your hands — a small but effective bit of immersion.

In that same vein, Rockstar also goes all in on haptic feedback to great effect. When you’re swimming, for example, you can feel each individual stroke Jason or Lucia takes. Again, much of the game feels like it was designed with that level of detail in mind. When cloning a car key, you’ll need to move the right joystick around in a circle and find the strongest vibration point. As you can imagine, haptic feedback only makes that minigame that much more tactile.

Even the DualSense’s adaptive triggers get put to good use. Step on the gas in a car, and you’ll get a hit of resistance that simulates the feeling of stepping on a gas pedal. Crack open a shipping container with a saw, and you’ll need to very carefully increase pressure on the right trigger to make the cut. Stop to meditate, and you’ll feel the triggers rattle under your fingers as you press them to breathe in and out. Every little minigame interaction plays with the triggers or feedback in some way.

The more I played, the more GTA 6 reminded me of early-generation PS5 tech showpieces; it has the same toy-like quality that Returnal and Astro’s Playroom had in the early PS5 years. While there have been plenty of third-party games that have integrated the DualSense in their own ways, GTA 6 has the most fully realized implementation of its features outside of Sony’s first-party games. That’s why it almost feels like an exclusive; six years into the PS5’s life, we finally have the game that really sells how the tech.

None of that is necessary to enjoy GTA 6, mind you. The extra feedback is a great perk if you own a PS5 already, but you’re not going to miss anything because your in-game phone rings from your TV speakers instead of your controller. The Xbox Series X will likely get the job done, and you might even prefer it if you don’t love the occasional strain that comes with adaptive triggers. But when Sony says that GTA 6 plays best on PS5, it’s not exactly a bluff. It does, but "play” is the key word there. It’s not that it looks or runs the best on PS5. It’s just the best platform for those who love toying around with their games.

#3421. How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

James Gray never hid that Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway were playing fictional versions of his real-life parents in his 2022 drama “Armageddon Time,” based on the writer/director’s experience as a sixth grader growing up in Queens in the 1980s.

“Jeremy is doing my father to such a degree that it is disturbing.  He sounds exactly like him, looks exactly like him; it’s bizarre. Annie, too, is uncanny about [playing my mother],” said Gray while a guest on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “So I had had such a great time with them shooting ‘Armageddon Time,’ I said, ‘Well, why don’t we do this again?’” Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Gray knew his next film (what would become “Paper Tiger”) would be set in 1986 and once again focus on a Jewish family of four, with two sons, in Queens. In the project’s early stages, Hathaway and Strong were up for reprising their roles, but it soon became clear Gray would have to wait 18 months — after both “The Odyssey” (Hathaway) and “The Social Reckoning” (Strong) finished filming — to start production.

“You can’t wait a year and a half,” said Gray. “And then I started thinking, ‘Well, maybe this is a blessing in disguise.’ That the [film] could start to take on a new style, and so then I started to pursue it in a different way. So in the beginning, in its origin stages, it was [a sequel of sorts], but like any movie, it’s like a wild horse that’s going to get away from you.”

While Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller’s characters in “Paper Tiger” are inspired by Gray’s parents, they are not as deeply grounded as Hathaway and Strong were in “Armageddon Time” as facsimiles of Gray’s parents in how they talked, looked, dressed, and behaved. Through this lens, Gray began to see the film as less of a straight memoir, freeing him to embrace elements of the crime genre in his storytelling.

Explained Gray, “What I tried to do was to make a film more in — for lack of a better way of really explaining — a bit more Hitchcockian in certain places. Almost — again, ‘pulpy’ is not quite the right word — a little bit more, how do I put this — more of an engagement directly with a tense idea of narrative, that it would be a driving, tense story.”

What also changed is the sympathetic lens through which Gray now saw his father. In “Paper Tiger,” Irwin (Teller) puts his family in danger when he unwittingly gets entangled (pursuing environmental consulting work for businesses along the polluted Gowanus Canal) with the Russian mob. While Irwin is guilty of pride and naivety, it is (especially compared to Gray’s previous films) a positive portrayal of a hard-working and earnest father pursuing the American dream.

In this sense, the shift from Strong to Teller was fortuitous. Strong had painted an unforgiving portrait of a miserable, strict father — tortured by generational trauma and unbending with his sons striving for upward mobility — whereas Gray saw something in Teller he could lean into for a different portrayal of his father.

“Miles has a kind of — I can’t believe I’m going to say this, he might even resist this— a softness to him, which would probably offend him, but I think that’s a great thing,” said Gray. “He doesn’t have a softness in his persona. He doesn’t have it in physical terms. It’s actually a tenderness inside. You have to embrace [that] beauty in him and hope it works for the film.”

When it came to recasting Hathaway, Gray was more practical, saying he needed three characteristics: another bankable star, who was also Jewish, and a real New Yorker. He believed the way the city seeps itself into a person’s bones is not something that even the best actors can learn to portray. Those three unnotiables made Scarlett Johansson the clear number one choice.

“I had met [Scarlett] years before on a project that never wound up happening, and quite liked her. She’s a total New Yorker through and through. Then when I found out that Annie [Hathaway] was going off to do Chris [Nolan’s] movie [‘The Odyssey’] for a thousand years, she was the first choice because you’re talking about one of the biggest stars in the world, and she’s also a Jewish woman from New York,  checks the boxes,” said Gray. “When I sent [the script] to her, I sent her a note, ‘There’s probably no chance in hell you’re going to do this, but I love you, can you read this?’ And then she texted me back very, very quickly and was like, ‘Let’s go.’”

While Hathaway’s portrayal of Gray’s mother was more open and loving than Strong’s version of his father — and therefore didn’t require as sharp a contrast in how the role was recast — Gray believed Johansson’s approach better fit the needs of “Paper Tiger.”

“It’s a more operatic idea of character than Annie’s was in ‘Armageddon Time,’” said Gray. “It’s much more a kind of high emotion. And of course, because the situation is much more tragic, and she embraced it completely.”

“Paper Tiger” opened last weekend in New York and Los Angeles, and expands on November 20.

#3420. The 8 Best Fantasy Book Authors of All Time, Ranked

Fantasy has been present in stories for just about as long as human storytelling has been a thing, but it didn't become an actual marketing label for the publishing industry until around the 19th century. Since then, we have gotten thousands of authors who can be called full-on fantasy authors, and there is many an element that makes up a great one. Without boundless imagination, deep technical craft, a purposeful eye for world-building, and the ability to write grounded characters, no fantasy author can be truly great.

But even though there have been hundreds upon hundreds of great fantasy writers over the years, there are eight in particular who can be considered the very best to ever grace the genre. These are authors who aren't just phenomenal from a technical or artistic standpoint, they are also of vital historical importance to the genre, still influencing countless fantasy authors the world over to this day. Their work is as foundational as it is essential, and their names belong on the bookshelf of all fantasy fans.

After graduating with a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the University of Manitoba, Canadian author Guy Gavriel Kay began writing poetry before turning to prose. Soon enough, he became one of the greatest—and most underrated—fantasy authors of his generation, penning many forgotten books that have aged like fine wine. His work has been particularly important in revolutionizing the mixture between fantasy and settings strongly resembling real historical places and periods, even though Kay himself rejects the label of historical fantasy.

Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion.

Before he published a single novel of his own, Kay was hired by Christopher Tolkien to help assemble and edit J. R. R. Tolkien's chaotic mass of posthumous manuscripts into the legendary The Silmarillion, and that alone should already be proof enough of his quality. After that, he became a true pioneer of inserting historical elements into the high fantasy genre, delivering masterpieces of the caliber of Tigana and The Lions of Al-Rassan.

Robin Hobb is the pen name of Margaret Astrid Lindholm Ogden, who's undoubtedly best known for her iconic Realm of the Elderlings megaseries. It wasn't until she turned 30 that she published her first book under the name of Megan Lindholm, proving that it's never too late to join the pantheon of history's greatest fantasy authors. She began writing as Robin Hobb 12 years later, and her debut under that legendary pen name was Assassin's Apprentice, the first book in the Farseer trilogy from the Realm of the Elderings series.

Exploring themes like otherness, gender, and queerness across her incredible work, Hobb has crafted some of the fantasy books with the best world-building and the best character writing in history. Shifting the genre's focus from earth-shattering spectacle to deep psychological intimacy and philosophical complexity, she proved just how character- and theme-driven the genre could be when written by a gifted enough author.

If there's any one author worthy of being called the most prolific and widely celebrated fantasy writer currently working, it's almost undeniably Brandon Sanderson. His debut novel, Elantris, was published in 2005, by the time Sanderson had already written about a dozen unpublished books. He has been nothing but a writing machine since then, best known for his iconic Cosmere universe. Composed of multiple subseries and standalones, it's one of the best ongoing fantasy book series.

From the Mistborn series to the Stormlight Archive, Sanderson has written several of the most ambitious high fantasy books of all time, all the while building the biggest multi-decade meta-narrative that fantasy literature has thus far seen. Off the page, he has also trained and influenced countless authors over the years, and coined the distinction between hard magic and soft magic systems, being the undisputed master of the former.

British author, literary scholar, and Anglican lay theologian C. S. Lewis also wrote some incredible science fiction, but he's obviously better known for his fantasy work, particularly The Chronicles of Narnia, one of those fantasy series where every book's a masterpiece. He began writing fiction as a child, inventing stories with his brother and fellow author, Warren Lewis; and soon enough became one of the most important English writers of his generation.

Alongside his good friend Tolkien, Lewis still stands as one of the major pillars of modern fantasy. His work not only revolutionized and popularized portal fantasy, it also made fantasy as a whole more widely accessible, more culturally ubiquitous, and more deeply rooted in Western mythology and philosophy than ever before. Without authors like him, who's to say whether fantasy would have ever been fully legitimized as a genre worthy of being taken seriously?

Another instance of a fantasy literature legend who's best known for one particular series, but whose contributions to the genre extend far beyond that, Robert Jordan is the must-read author of some of the most perfectly-written fantasy books in history. He decided that he wanted to write books while recovering from his time as a Vietnam War veteran, and began writing while working as a nuclear engineer for the US Navy.

High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about.

The most prominent work of such an iconic career is The Stormlight Archive, far and away one of the greatest and most influential fantasy book series since the '90s. High fantasy had been very heavily inspired by Tolkien (or directly aiming to imitate him) for decades before Jordan came about, and it was authors like him who proved that the genre could start doing things differently. Darker, more mature, and more complex than most other fantasy novels from his time, Jordan's work broke the mold and has continued aging like fine wine.

Dramatic fantasy is of vital importance, and it's always a delight to read an author who actually takes the genre seriously and builds something deeply compelling out of it. However, comedic fantasy is arguably every bit as important, and as far as that subgenre goes, you don't get any authors more foundational than Sir Terry Pratchett, fantasy's most beloved satirist. He's best known for his Discworld series, composed of a whopping 41 fantasy comedies.

What makes Pratchett's work so brilliant is that even though his satirical fantasy works are undeniably hilarious, they're also surprisingly profound. On top of providing one of the best soft magic systems in history, Discworld proved that even comedic fantasy could be legitimately serious in its own way. Thematically complex and richly human, Pratchett's work interrogates human nature, institutions, and morality in all sorts of enrapturing ways. His books are brilliantly meta and quite diverse, making Discworld a must-read series for anyone who thinks that fantasy can't be hilarious and profound at the same time.

In the entire history of speculative fiction, few authors have ever been quite as important as Ursula K. Le Guin. Indeed, the American master could also very reasonably be counted among the eight most important and essential sci-fi authors of all time, but there are many who prefer her work in fantasy. Le Guin wrote her first fantasy story at age nine and submitted her first sci-fi story to a magazine at age 11, and from there, there was nowhere for her to go but up.

The daughter of an anthropologist and with a deep academic interest in mythology, Le Guin wrote masterpieces like Lavinia and the Earthsea Cycle, many of them among those books that are a masterclass in high fantasy writing. By introducing elements of Taoist philosophy, psychological realism, and non-Eurocentric anthropological and cultural depth to her work, Le Guin completely rejected many of the tropes and traditions that had ruled fantasy literature for years. She genuinely revolutionized fantasy, pioneering many new tropes of her own in the process.

You'd be hard-pressed to find anyone unwilling to call J. R. R. Tolkien the single greatest and most influential fantasy author of modern times, and that's for good reason. Never has the history of speculative fiction seen anybody quite like Tolkien, and it likely never will again. Sparked by the Professor's love for philology, ancient mythologies, and original myth-making, the world was treated to an authorial career that completely revolutionized fantasy. Indeed, many would divide the genre's modern history between the pre-Tolkien and the post-Tolkien eras.

Yes, Tolkien wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, his most celebrated works and perhaps the most influential fantasy novels of the 20th century. However, his contributions to the genre extend far beyond. He wrote several masterworks outside Middle-earth, he contributed to the academic study of fantasy, and he completely laid down the blueprint for modern high, epic, and heroic fantasies. Author of some of the most memorable characters, the most fascinating lore, and the best battles in the history of fantasy books, Tolkien was the greatest of all fantasy writers. It will take someone so special that he's truly out of this world to ever dethrone Tolkien.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

#3419. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

From a purely awards-hunting perspective, there’s a great argument to be made that Netflix could have pushed back its late November release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” until next year. Historically, the perception of the embattled studio is that its had issues being distracted by too big an awards slate to pin down its Best Picture frontrunner. Remember in 2023 when it seemed like the streamer did not realize until the Oscar shortlists (in mid-December!) that “All Quiet on the Western Front” was its best bet at Best Picture? The Edward Berger film went on to win four Oscars, including Best International Feature. Related Stories How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

This year, Netflix is running their best awards campaign yet with “La Bola Negra,” which the studio acquired out of Cannes, where its helmers, Los Javis, won the jury prize for Best Director. Come the fall festivals, it became the first Netflix film to win the People’s Choice Award at TIFF. Since then, it has fronted Netflix’s experiment in expanding the theatrical distribution of its awards slate, doing admirable business in key markets. The consensus among prognosticators is that the film is not only a lock to receive a Best Picture nomination, but is also sure to win the Oscar for Best International Feature on behalf of Spain.

If Netflix wanted to secure a second Best Picture nomination, with “Cliff Booth” out of the picture, the team could put all its energy into Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” Not only is the near-three hour film, which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, another Best International Feature contender (on behalf of South Korea), but it is one of this season’s most critically lauded films. If enough critics’ groups get behind it in the coming weeks, a la “The Secret Agent” last year, then a second Best Picture nomination for Netflix at the 2027 Oscars becomes highly plausible.

Somewhere along the way, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” became something of a puzzle for Netflix. The streamer had no choice but to follow through with putting it out around Thanksgiving, because it was already set to replace the IMAX screens that had initially been secured for Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film. So how does a company not run an awards campaign for the sequel to a recent Best Picture nominee, directed by a three-time Oscar nominee, written by a two-time Oscar winner, and starring Brad Pitt in the role he just won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for?

What reads as a home run on paper is more of a double or triple in execution. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is made by people who know what they are doing, and that expands past director David Fincher, screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, and star Pitt.

Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt, editor Kirk Baxter, production designer Donald Graham Burt, set decorator Jan Pascale, and composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have all won at least one Academy Award. Costume designer Trish Summerville was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Mank.” Even if there is a low bar for getting the Academy excited about a late-’70s period piece set in Hollywood, “Cliff Booth” easily clears it.

But we are in a spectacle-heavy year, with “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” in the awards conversation, and “Dune: Part Three” and “Werwulf” on the horizon. Even “Digger” is a formidable contender in the craft races. So if the feeling is that “Cliff Booth” is more of a hangout movie than a cinematic event, then the focus of its awards campaign should be on categories that are more willing to embrace that, like Best Production Design or Best Costume Design. (Not so much Best Sound, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did actually receive nominations for.)

In terms of the acting performances, again, Pitt is great as Cliff Booth, but there is no rush to nominate him for a performance he already won for. And there are plenty of other Best Actor contenders, like Matt Damon and John Malkovich (who have never won) and John Turturro and Andrew Scott (who have never even been nominated for an Oscar before).

The top performance of the film is with Cliff’s love interest, played by Emmy winner Elizabeth Debicki, who actually does have a shot at her first Oscar nomination, given the love for her performance in “Wicker” as well, and the lack of current consensus in the Best Supporting Actress race.

Everyone else in the film, from Scott Caan to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II to Carla Gugino, is very additive to the project but does not necessarily cross the threshold into Oscar-contender territory. In that way, it is similar to Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” another awards hopeful from this season.

Ultimately, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is entertaining enough to garner support from certain branches of the Academy, but falls too late in the year, in too few theaters, to truly become the last-minute surprise blockbuster that would get as many as 10 Oscar nominations, something its predecessor “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did handily.

#3418. GTA 6: How To Unlock Selling Cars

There are multiple ways to earn money in GTA 6, and not all of them are as efficient. While robbing smaller stores can be less risky than robbing a major bank, the yield is also low, and you still need to clean/fence that merchandise afterward.

In that sense, stealing and selling cars can be even easier to do, but you need to go about it the right way. Plus, you can't just sell cars at the start of the game. You'll need to work up Jason and Lucia's contacts, and eventually find someone who will take stolen vehicles for cash later in the game.

After entering Chapter 2, you'll take full control of Lucia, as you're whisked away to a hotel in the northwest corner of the map. This zone is fairly relaxed, with minimal organized gang activity and lots of woods to lose the cops in.

After completing the first few story missions with Lucia, you'll meet a mutual friend named Moses, who operates out of a garage and junkyard. Moses will walk you through the tutorial for stealing cars and returning them.

You won't be able to steal a car right outside of Moses' shop and turn it in for cash.

Moses will also provide you with the Slim Jim item, which makes stealing cars a lot easier. To use the Slim Jim, you'll press Triangle (Y on Xbox) instead of Square (X on Xbox) to smash the window. From there, you'll need to do another analog-stick-shifting minigame to fully pop the lock, then enter the vehicle without incident.

You can use the Slim Jim for the rest of GTA 6 with both characters. There's no need to equip it or anything; it'll automatically be part of Jason and Lucia's loadout. Keep it in mind if you're trying to steal a car, as it makes less noise and many car alarms don't even go off.

To get paid for stealing cars, drive a car back to Moses, bring it into his shop (the garage door will open), then speak to Moses directly. Make sure you use the L2 method (LT on Xbox) to focus on Moses, and bring up more dialogue options. This will let you sell the car to him directly, so you can complete the transaction.

Note that more expensive cars provide bigger yields, and you can search cars for their worth using the Waink app (the shortcut is holding up on the d-pad). Try to go for bigger sales and avoid picking up junky cars, as it'll only take more time to make a ton of cash.

Also, keep in mind that the Slim Jim is pretty much your main tool for stealing cars until later in the game, when you unlock the key cloner. Once you have that, you can steal higher-end cars with advanced security systems for even bigger profits.

As you progress through the game, Moses isn't the only person who will buy cars off of you. More vendors await in later portions of GTA 6, so you won't need to drive all the way to Moses to make a delivery.
