#3324. Here’s one small change that could improve iPhone Duo’s unoptimized apps

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an issue.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

So, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#3323. Rod Wave Indicted for Allegedly Carrying Oxycodone and a Gun While Speeding

Rap star Rod Wave has been indicted on felony drug and weapons possession charges in Georgia.

According to the Fulton County indictment obtained by Rolling Stone, the 28-year-old artist unlawfully possessed Oxycodone and had a gun “within arm’s reach” when he was pulled over for reckless driving on Nov. 7, 2025. The indictment alleges Wave, whose legal name is Rodarius Green, was driving at least 15 miles over the posted speed limit and disregarded a “traffic control device” in a “highly residential area” of Atlanta along Defoor Ave. The indictment was returned Oct. 30 and unsealed this month.

A lawyer for Wave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Green was originally booked on reckless driving and drug and gun possession charges and released the following day, according to online jail records. He allegedly had a black .40 caliber Glock with a high-capacity magazine in his waistband when he was taken into custody, according to Atlanta News First.

The arrest came the same day Green earned his first-ever Grammy nomination, for Best Song Written for Visual Media, for his track “Sinners” from the 2025 film of the same name. He and his fellow nominees lost the award to “Golden” from KPop Demon Hunters at the February ceremony. #3322. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

When you can't sleep, you'll try anything to drift off. But I can almost guarantee you've never tried something like the Spatial Sleep Headband. This peculiar wearable uses acoustic resonance to send you snoozing. I put it to the test and yes, it's as weird as it sounds.

Type: Sleep headbandBest for: Insomnia, trouble falling asleepDimensions: 4" x 7.8" x 3.7"Weight: 2.5 ozWarranty: 90 days limitedPrice: $319 at SoundHealth

The Spatial Sleep Band sits on your forehead where it vibrates and plays sound. With regular use this combo should train your brain's neural response to build better sleep, no hard work required. Although I'll be honest, the Spatial Sleep Band isn't what I'd describe as easy.

I used the Spatial Sleep headband nightly for four weeks and I'll dive into my full experience below. In brief, it's an odd sensation and one that comes with a steep learning curve. And while eventually the Spatial Sleep Band does become a soothing addition to your bedtime routine, it's a struggle to get to that point.

As someone with only mild sleep issues, I've yet to see any real benefit from the Spatial Sleep Band. And the adjustment period was frustrating enough that I'd have given up if it wasn't my job to keep going. For those with more severe sleep problems, the annoyance of the Spatial Sleep Headband will likely feel like less of an intrusion, and the benefits more noticeable.

But it's an expensive gamble, with a Spatial Sleep Headband costing $319 (although that's slightly more affordable than similar sleep headbands like the Muse S Athena and the Elemind). You do get a 45-day return period as well, and by that point you should have a good idea if this product is for you. And it's subscription-free — that's rare for this kind of sleep tech.

The Spatial Sleep Headband costs $319 — an investment, for sure, but this is a fairly standard price tag for a high-tech sleep aid. There's no subscription required and a 45-day returns policy is included.

The overall design of the Spatial Sleep Headband is relatively simple. The slim band is made from a soft material and the Velcro strap is easy to adjust.

Its secret lies on the inside, where you'll find two purple nodules. These press against the forehead and deliver the acoustic vibration that makes the Spatial Headband work.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There's one more important part to the Spatial and that's the three lines on the front of the design. These are used to align the band with the center of your face, to ensure the sound is delivered to the right part of the forehead.

I used the Spatial Sleep Headband for four weeks as part of my usual routine, wearing it to bed (with an eye mask). Here's how I rate the performance...

Setting up the Spatial Sleep Headband is simple, for a piece of complex tech. First you have to charge it, then turn the headband on (there's a button on the front) and connect it to the app.

You'll be asked to scan your face — this helps Spatial create a sound just right for you. When you're ready to sleep, get the band in position and press start on the app.

The sound automatically plays for 45 minutes, at which point you should be asleep (fingers crossed). You can pause and restart the sound from the app, in case of late night wake ups.

The battery lasts for roughly 90 minutes, or two sessions, and I have used mine through two nights without charging. However, I recommend charging after every session, to avoid the sound cutting out. A USB-C cable is provided and charging takes roughly 30 minutes.

The app is mostly used to kick off the audio at night, but there's a fun memory game you can play as well.

I'm normally game for testing any kind of weird sleep tech but when I first strapped the Spatial Band to my head, I felt like I'd made a terrible mistake. Nodules pressed into my forehead and my bones rattled to a dissonant hum that sounded like pans clattering to the ground in the distance. I clenched my jaw and waited for it to end.

There was an important lesson here, echoed in the bright red dents on my forehead: do not over-tighten the band.

With a slightly looser band, night two went better. But the first week was rough. The sound and sensations of the Spatial Headband are far removed from my usual sleep comforts. I was hoping using it would help me drift off quickly but instead I lay awake, questioning the life choices that had led me to this moment.

Spatial does warn that it takes persistence before you see results and week two went better. The sound and I had gotten used to each other, meaning it no longer sat at the forefront of my mind. Now I enjoyed a pleasant background hum and only occasionally worried about my vibrating skull.

By week three I could see a glimmer of progress. The distant drone of the sleep headband had grown relaxing. One night, on the brink of sleep, I even found myself wondering what the pleasant noise was.

These benefits have yet to be reflected in my sleep score, however. On some nights it still takes me up upwards of 30 minutes to drift off fully. And I'm still experiencing brief wake ups in the night. (Including waking up to take the headband off — the nodules are uncomfortable when they press against your face.)

Last night, having reached the end of my four weeks testing period, I decided to ditch the headband and go back to my usual sleep patterns. I got an 88 sleep score from my Oura Ring, my highest in 12 nights.

As someone with only minor sleep problems, the Spatial Sleep Headband is a steep learning curve for a small advantage. But I don't want to write it off entirely. There are strong reviews from other users and Spatial has conducted some notable research. Spatial is designed to improve your natural sleep frequency, so for those who have a sleep routine that's completely off-beat, the Spatial sleep might help set the pace you need.

The Spatial Headband uses acoustic vibrations and sleep-friendly frequencies to improve the quality and quantity of your sleep. It requires regular use to see the results and after several weeks the strange hum of the Spatial should be the backdrop to a decent night's rest.

The problem is that those first weeks are challenging, to put it mildly. From the sound to the feel, the Spatial band is simply strange to use. It feels like a disruptive force and you might be tempted to give up before you feel the benefits. Or rather, if you feel the benefits — I stuck with mine and noticed only minor differences.

✅ You're experiencing long-term sleep deprivation: The Spatial Sleep Headband didn't work for me but it is backed by some serious research. Its impact might be more noticeable when overcoming bigger sleep problems.

✅ You've tried all kinds of sleep tech and nothing works: Acoustic resonance is unusual and not the kind of sleep enhancer you pick up on a whim. If you're struggling to improve your sleep, this might be worth a try.

✅ You're kept awake by disruptive noise: When the Spatial band is on, it drowns out most other sounds. That's good news if traffic or rowdy neighbors are contributing to your sleep problems.

❌ You want a quick solution: Spatial suggests it takes three to four weeks to feel the benefit of the Sleep Headband, and I found week one to be a steep learning curve. The Muse S Athena sleep headband was much easier to get used to.

❌ You share a bed with a light sleeper: Some sound does leak from the Spatial headband which might disturb co-sleepers.

❌ You want a small sleep boost, rather than a total overhaul: For minor sleep issues the Spatial Sleep Band is a pricey investment that takes time to get used to. Try low-cost options like sleepy tea and guided meditations before diving in with the Spatial.

The Muse S Athena uses your brainwaves to track your sleep and, when it senses you're about to be disturbed, plays a sleep-inducing sound to send you back under. I tested it and found the performance impressive but it is a premium buy, retailing for $479.99 at Muse and Amazon.

The Snoozeband isn't as high-tech as the other options listed here but this comfortable set of sleep headphones can help you drift off in noisy environments. It utilizes thin speakers in a soft headband to deliver sleep sounds without the discomfort of an earbud. From $49.99 at Snoozeband.

#3317. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3313. New camera sensor coming to the iPhone 20 Pro’s main camera, says leaker

The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear …

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an issue with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a new sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

(Under Apple’s current naming system, next year’s iPhone Pro would be the iPhone 19 Pro. However, it’s widely expected that Apple will jump to the iPhone 20 nomenclature in order to mark a significant design upgrade for the 20th anniversary of the device.)

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.

#3311. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3310. Microsoft outage saw 80% of servers fail – here’s what happened

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected …

The company said at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs announced the previous month.

Users were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two issues. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […]

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

#3309. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3306. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3305. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3304. Apple has renewed Slow Horses for seasons 7, 8, 9, and 10

Slow Horses isn’t going away anytime soon, as Apple TV confirmed today that the hit series has been renewed through season 10—meaning at least four more seasons are coming.

The era of streaming TV has often been marked by shows being canceled too soon, and taking long breaks between seasons.

Slow Horses is a stark exception on both fronts. The British spy series premiered in 2022, and Apple TV recently finished airing its sixth season.

Apple has made a practice of ordering more Slow Horses seasons far sooner than most shows get renewed. Viewers now expect that at the end of one season, a trailer for the next season will debut.

But today Apple has extended Slow Horses far beyond what’s typical. Via Deadline, the company confirmed that Slow Horses has been renewed for seasons 9 and 10.

The latest approvals join the already-approved seasons 7 and 8.

It’s very rare for any show to run for 10 or more seasons. But it’s perhaps even harder to find a series that’s picked up for four additional seasons in advance.

Slow Horses season 6 wrapped up last month, and now fans know that there are at least four more seasons coming—likely with the same annual premiere cadence.

Are you a Slow Horses fan, and do you think the show could keep going on indefinitely? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

Google and Xreal's spatial computing AR glasses have finally arrived and I've been wearing them for just a few days. They're an interesting hint at the future of both computing and wearables.

In the smart glasses space, there isn't anything like the Aura's. They're not quite a VR headset, but they're far more advanced than display glasses like Xreal's own One Pro Plus.

Xreal's only potential rivals exist in tech that has yet to actually hit shelves: the Snap Specs (which are supposed to ship "this fall") and the Meta VR Glasses that don't drop until sometime in Spring 2027.

There's a lot going on here, and we'll have a full review soon, but here are some early first impressions. As we dig into the glasses, if there's something you want to know reach out to scott.younker@futurenet.com or leave a comment below!

Beyond the puck, the Xreal Aura glasses won't look out of place next to any other display spectacles made by the company. There is an aesthetic to this kind of glasses and you can see it mirrored in Xreal's rival Viture with the recent Pro 2 glasses.

Where you'll notice the difference is in the cameras. Like the best smart glasses, the Aura features cameras at the temples plus one on the nose bridge. These are built to enable the gesture controls and 6DoF spatial computing, something no other Xreal glasses have natively.

The Aura sits somewhat between Meta's VR Glasses and Snap Specs; mostly, it comes down to software and cameras. Meta glasses have more cameras that can "see" your hands even if they're in your lap.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the Aura's, moving your hands down to your lap means you're most likely using the puck as a trackpad, which works pretty well.

The puck is a computer for the glasses thanks to the powerful Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset. If you work in the Google suite, you have access to all of the Google apps and services you could want. Plus, it comes with Gemini AI, which you can access via voice controls.

Nicely, you don't need the puck for mirroring. You can connect the glasses to any device, save the Switch 2 (more on that below), and they will work like your normal Xreal glasses.

If you've worn a pair of Xreal glasses, the Aura feels about the same. I think they're fairly comfortable, and they do come with different nose pad sizes. Plus, the arms can be adjusted by three levels, which helps settle the glasses.

I want to highlight the speakers in the Aura. I hate speakers in display glasses and often find them tinny, preferring to use headphones. Also, especially since I travel or use the glasses to not disturb my partner at night even if the speakers are siloed, sound still leaks out.

Now, the Bose speakers in the Aura won't beat the best headphones, but they sound way better than any other glasses I've tested.

The included puck has both the computing chipsets and the battery. The puck is about the size of a thick iPhone 16, and does have some heft. You could use the included belt clip so that you don't have to hold the puck when you're out and about (which gives cellphone belt guy vibes).

The Xreal Aura are rated for about 3 hours of continuous use. I haven't done a full rundown test yet, but in my usage I've found that to be fairly accurate.

Perhaps that's for the best. I've found that the portion of the glasses that rests on your eyebrows gets warm. Not uncomfortably so, but noticeably enough that I wonder how that settles out over the long term. The puck, however, does seem to dissipate heat fairly well, and I never felt it get warm.

Xreal partnered with Google on the Aura and you can feel Mountain View's presence in the Android XR platform that lives in the puck. If you've ever tested the Samsung Galaxy XR headset, then you've seen the Android XR interface before.

It's the exact same here, with fewer capabilities thanks to fewer cameras and a little less power. The Aura also has a smaller FOV of 70 degrees. VR enthusiasts won't like that, but I think most people will find it more than usable.

You can use pinch gestures or the trackpad puck to control the interface. So far I've found the gesture controls smooth and intuitive. The Aura comes with a delightful setup process that teaches you how to use the gesture controls and puck so you can open the glasses up ready to go. It's honestly one of the better startup tutorials I've come across.

In previous hands-on sessions, the gesture controls felt a bit laggy at times, but whatever work Xreal and Google have done in the meantime has really made the controls much better.

Honestly, it's not as exciting as the eye-tracking in the Meta VR Glasses, but it works well, so I'm not knocking it too much.

Since the system runs on Android XR there are a lot of AR (and some VR-lite) games that you can play on the Aura. Xreal recommended the excellent Demeo, which is available in the Play Store.

I've already enjoyed Demeo in VR and the AR translation is a delight, using pinch controls to move the map, zoom in, and make choices. You'll need to pay attention to your hand position so the cameras can catch it.

I do think you'll need a controller to enjoy the most out of what the Aura can do or a mouse and keyboard. Fortunately, you can connect a surprising number of accessories to the Aura via Bluetooth (more on that below).

But what makes the Aura standout is the connectivity. As mentioned, you can just use the glasses to run a Steam Deck or mirror using a cable on your laptop. Have I been running WoW: Forever through the Aura glasses? Yes. Should I? That remains to be seen.

We got a sneak peek during AWE 2026 back in June, but the Xreal Aura is one of the few glasses that can connect to the Switch 2. Compared to the mini dock and larger pro dock that Viture makes, the Aura puck is lighter, smaller and does more than just act as a passthrough and battery pack. And it does so through the USB-C connection into the puck.

It's a delight to pop in Mario Kart World or the Ocarina of Time remake on the glasses. I still don't know how Xreal and Qualcomm got this to work, but I'm happy it does.

Xreal has said that you can accessorize the Aura with peripherals to enhance your use. With that in mind, the company did send us a wireless gaming controller built by GameSir, a wireless folding keyboard and a USB-C DP-in for mirroring external devices.

All three add an extra cost on top of the initial $1,299 glasses price. The GameSir controller costs $99 and can be used wirelessly or wired and has an AI button.

GameSir makes good controllers and the Xreal one is pretty decent. However, if you already have an Xbox, PlayStation or other Bluetooth controller, the Aura will support them. You won't have the Gemini button, but if you're like me and don't use that anyway, it shouldn't be a problem.

The Xreal keyboard is $79 but comes with Aura-specific keys in the FN row that enable you to control the glasses like you would your monitor on a laptop. It's actually a pretty comfortable keyboard, and the foldability for travel makes it an excellent companion. Honestly, so far you should add the $79 as part of the cost of getting a pair of Auras. You can also pair it with other devices, including laptops and tablets.

The cable is a Silkland USB-C one that costs $12.99. If you already have a USB-C DP in cable, it should work, but you're not out too much if you're looking to do wired mirroring.

At over $1,000, the Xreal Aura is pretty expensive, but these glasses are a lot of compute shrunk down into a pair of glasses and a cell phone-sized puck.

I don't know that everyone needs these glasses, and it's not quite the super portable laptop replacement yet, but it is an exciting glimpse at the future of AR glasses. Between the Aura, Snap Specs, and Meta VR Glasses the next generation of glasses has some true potential.

There's also room for the Aura to grow from both a software and hardware perspective.

We're not there yet, but the Aura feels like a true step toward the sci-fi eyewear that we saw in movies and shows as kids.

#3302. HomeView missing some podcast feeds? Here’s why

Apple’s new HomeView features the Podcasts app, but not all feeds appear to be supported for now. Instead, HomeView appears to have the same bug that tvOS 27 introduced to the Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

tvOS 27.0 added playback support for HLS-based video podcasts on Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

The same update introduced a bug that dropped support for syncing shows manually added via URL.

The new Apple HomeView appears to have this same bug. Video podcasts using HLS technology are supported, but shows added via URL do not work.

As of tvOS 27.3 beta 1, the bug is still present on Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and newer.

Because tvOS 27 doesn’t run on Apple TV 4K 1st-gen, URL-based subscriptions still work in the Podcasts app — just not HLS-based video feeds.

Anyway, if you’re missing certain feeds in the Podcasts app on HomeView, this is likely the reason.

#3301. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3300. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

With user permission, ChatGPT Health connects to Apple Health and supported medical records to provide useful context to health-related questions. The feature currently works in the United States on iPhone, iPad, and the web.

For instance, ChatGPT Health will soon work with the desktop version of ChatGPT for the first time. This would bring ChatGPT Health to the Mac app.

OpenAI also says ChatGPT Health will work with Android, ChatGPT Sites, and ChatGPT Dots, the company’s proactive assistant feature.

The move follows a similar pattern with the rollout of ChatGPT Finances, which was originally limited to mobile and the web before recently reaching the Mac app as well.

No official timing yet for when ChatGPT Health will expand, but OpenAI notified users about the upcoming expansion earlier this month.

#3296. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.
