#3278. The Irresistible Alchemy of Man / Woman / Chainsaw

W hatever you do, do not ask the six musicians in Man/Woman/Chainsaw which one of them is the chainsaw.

“Don’t do it,” warns singer Vera Leppänen, looking deadly serious. “We’ve heard that one so many times.”

“It’s so annoying,” says her bandmate Billy Doyle, shaking his head.

Billy Ward, another bandmate, agrees: “Don’t ask about the name.”

Luckily, the name is far from the most interesting thing about this fast-rising, fantastically original London group. Their first full-length album, Cannonball, collides all kinds of sounds that really shouldn’t go together — vulnerable folk, head-banging hard rock, a bit of classical, a little dance music, several genuinely enormous pop hooks — and, somehow, it works like a charm every single time. It’s a magic trick that gets more remarkable with every replay. When we saw Man/Woman/Chainsaw play at South By Southwest in March 2025, we called them “a young band in the process of inventing something ecstatically new.” Cannonball is what they invented, and sure enough, it’s one of this year’s most rewarding debuts.

The day after their first-ever New York show, the six of them have gathered in the backyard of a coffee shop in Bed-Stuy to chat with Rolling Stone. It’s our second choice for a meeting spot — the first café we tried had no room for a party of seven — but these young musicians are hardly bothered by a last-minute change of location. Leppänen (lead vocals and bass), Ward (lead vocals and guitar), Emmie-Mae Avery (lead vocals and keyboard), Clio Starwood (violin), Doyle (guitar), and Lola Cherry (drums), all aged 21, sit around a table in the sun, lighting rollies, laughing, and trading notes on last night’s gig.

“It’s funny,” Leppänen says. “America’s so far away for us, and they know our songs.”

“The music crossed the pond,” says Starwood.

“Yeah,” Ward says. “I walked past some people chatting at the bar, and they were talking about why they were there: ‘So I’m a really big Chainsaw fan…'” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

A few hours later, at the second stop on their U.S. tour, they show why their music has drawn such an enthusiastic audience in this country. It’s the night before Halloween, and the club is packed with costumed people who are ready to have fun — and Man/Woman/Chainsaw are more than happy to oblige. Up front, Ward and Leppänen rage like a pair of punk-rock demon twins. He growls theatrically on “The Thing” and “Goddamn, Lizard Man!,” and she slides with ease from the sullen fury of “Still Angry” to the pristine clarity of “Lighter.” Starwood shreds on her violin, Doyle brings a dash of jazzy style on guitar, and Cherry is a tireless dynamo behind the kit. Then there’s Avery, whose mellifluous vocals are indispensable to “Nosedive” — their biggest hit by far, with nearly 2.5 million Spotify plays — and their killer cover of the Breeders’ “Cannonball.” By the end of the night, the whole room is literally jumping.

Man/Woman/Chainsaw have been building toward this moment for about seven years. Ward and Leppänen were the first to meet, crossing paths at age 14 at the BRIT School, the performing-arts laboratory whose alumni include Adele, Amy Winehouse, Lola Young, and Olivia Dean. They spent the next few years assembling a backing band, which wasn’t too hard — “We knew a lot of people that played a lot of instruments,” Leppänen says — and booking gigs at local pubs. Related Content Who Gets to Own Rock & Roll History? No One Writes About Everyday Life Quite Like Star Moles How Bob Dylan’s Trip to London Inspired ‘Girl From the North Country’ Geese Never Thought They’d End Up Here

“We’d be in school, and Billy and Vera would come up to me at lunch and be like, ‘Do you want to go play the fucking Amersham Arms tonight?'” Avery recalls.

By the time they all turned 16 or 17, they were drawing attention for their wild live performances. (The band name, for the record, appears to be a reference to feminist film critic Carol J. Clover’s influential 1992 volume Men, Women, and Chainsaws, in which she identified the horror trope of the “final girl.”) And though Ward dismisses the music they were making at this point as “just noisy London bullshit,” they found a place in a scene that was regaining its bearings after the end of Covid restrictions.

“It’s such a privilege to be from a city that has so many venues, that has so many people that champion independent music,” Leppänen says. “We were very lucky to be able to just go out and do whatever.”

“We’d be on lineups with crazy noise rock, or post-punky stuff with a guy talking, or really electronic stuff,” Ward says. “There’s just such a variety.”

“It felt like you could do anything,” Cherry says.

Man/Woman/Chainsaw’s eclectic sound reflects the band’s democratic writing style, where anyone can make a suggestion and everyone will listen. It’s “the cocktail combination of six brains,” as Starwood puts it. And while many of them are fond of pop acts like Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo, and Lana Del Rey, they see no contradiction between those sounds and the others in their mix.

“A lot of the best rock music, even the artiest, weirdest, guitary-est music, has great pop choruses,” Ward says. “That’s a thing that pretty universally makes the song good, is having something you can come back to. It’s important.”

They spent about two years workshopping the songs on Cannonball before stepping into RAK Studios with producers Seth Evans and Margo Broom in the summer of 2025 to begin recording. All the while, most of them were attending university (all but Ward and Avery, who opted to focus on the band). As part of her degree, Leppänen wrote papers on subjects including the Irish rap trio Kneecap, for a class on music and politics. She mentions that she later met one of the members of that group — “I did tell him I wrote about him. He said, ‘You’re welcome.’ And he said I was charming” — which leads her to a story about the time they all ran into Lewis Capaldi at a Chainsaw show. “He said I was a boss,” she says.

“Both of these people were wasted when they gave these compliments,” Ward observes wryly. “So let’s take it with a pinch of salt.”

For another graduating requirement, Leppänen submitted a performance by Man/Woman/Chainsaw. “If people want to know if we’re a good band, the answer is yeah, we got a good mark,” says Starwood.

Some of the songs on the album began with a group jam, like “Only Girl,” the soaring anthem that opens Cannonball. “I just had two chords,” Ward says. “And a dream,” Leppänen says.

“We could tell that was going to be the first song on the album as soon as we wrote it,” Cherry adds. “When it feels right, you can tell, because we just want to play the song again and again and again.”

Others emerged more fully-formed, like “Still Angry,” which came from a voice note that Leppänen sent the band. “I played it to my mom,” Ward says. “I was like, ‘Listen to this shit. It’s a fucking amazing pop song. Vera’s done it again.'”

“Nosedive” came into focus near the end of the sessions. “We needed a couple more songs for our album, and we took names out of a hat and split into two groups,” Starwood recalls. In one room, the three lead singers — Leppänen, Ward, and Avery — wrote a vocal part by reworking an acoustic demo that Avery had brought in. In another, the three remaining members put together an instrumental arrangement that’s slower and softer than most Chainsaw songs, and entirely enchanting.

“We spent the rest of the evening just jamming it,” says Starwood, who remembers holding down a synth note with one foot while her hands were busy on violin. “It came together in such a satisfying way.”

Last winter, as they were putting the finishing touches on the album, several of the bandmates met in the studio to record backing vocals for the song. A few days later, after speaking with some students back at the BRIT School, Cherry heard the new mix with those group vocals for the first time. “It was so full-circle,” the drummer recalls. “It was so sweet. Tears in my eyes.”

“Nosedive” remains a highlight at their live shows, and they generally save it for the last spot in the set list. “Billy Ward’s dad got him for Christmas a bubble gun in the shape of a pink chainsaw, and Vera always wields it in that song,” Starwood says.

At a recent hometown gig at London’s Electric Ballroom, they took that peak even higher by detonating a confetti cannon during “Nosedive.” “It was a big bang,” Starwood says. “It was really loud.”

That does raise a potential problem for their shows next year, which include another run of bigger U.S. clubs in New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Austin, and Washington, D.C. in February.

“I don’t know how you top bubbles coming out of a pink chainsaw and confetti,” Starwood continues. “We can’t do the same thing twice. Dancers, maybe?” Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage

“Pyrotechnics,” Ward says. “That’s the word of the year, 2027: pyrotechnics.”

#3277. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3276. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

#3274. 10 Shows Like 'Youth' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3273. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3272. Kiss Finally Show Their Vulnerable Side in New Doc: ‘The Less Secrets You Have, the Freer You Are’

The first few minutes of the new documentary Kiss: End of the Road set up its next couple of hours. “We’re Superman with a guitar,” singer-guitarist Paul Stanley tells the camera. “Unfortunately, age is our kryptonite.” A few minutes later in the film, we see an exhausted Gene Simmons onstage at a 2023 gig in Manaus, Brazil, sweat dripping from his makeup as he collapses into a pile, catching his breath in a chair for several minutes. The scene was an inauspicious start to the first show of the final leg of the diehard rockers’ “absolute final shows.” The band’s manager, Doc McGhee, recalls in the film: “Paul said, ‘I’m out of here. I’m not gonna die up here.'”

When Stanley hears those words today, though, he smirks and spins them into a positive. He’s dressed down in a hoodie, sitting in his home office for a Zoom interview. “Seeing my brother Gene not only struggling but failing, I said, ‘That’s it,'” he recalls. “I said, ‘Regardless of what he wants to do, I owe it to him to pull the plug … certainly for the evening.'”

Simmons ultimately mustered the necessary strength to lift the 40 pounds of battle armor he was wearing and resume one of his signature songs, “Cold Gin.” After the show, in one of the stadium’s hallways, Simmons asks the cameraman, “Did you catch me throwing up?” which leads to McGhee conceding, “They’re showing their age.” Even though Simmons, Stanley, guitarist Tommy Thayer, and drummer Eric Singer were putting their all into performing tongue-waving, fire-breathing, ziplining, hard-rock hits like “Detroit Rock City,” “Lick It Up,” and “Love Gun,” rocking and rolling all night, let alone for a few hours, was beginning to look ambitious.

“If there’s such a thing as more than 100 percent humidity, it was there,” Simmons says today. He’s dressed entirely in black, including his baseball cap and sunglasses, to Zoom in from a solo tour stop somewhere on the Dakotas border. “Combined with very high temperatures approaching 100 degrees, you walk out and you’re just drenched. Stupid me, I didn’t drink enough liquids, so down I went.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Asked now what he thinks of Stanley’s impulse to pull the plug on the show, Simmons says, “Bitch, who do you think you’re talking to?”

Simmons and Stanley’s friendship remains brother-like, though, as one especially funny scene from the doc, premiering here exclusively, shows.

Simmons’ bravado about his rocky start in Brazil can’t overshadow the hard truths Kiss faced on the tour. The two-part doc, which premieres Thursday as a pay-per-view stream, occasionally feels like Spinal Tap: The band straightens out botched pyro cues, deals with a wardrobe malfunction when Stanley’s guitar gets hooked on his boot, and keeps playing while the streamers meant to burst out during “Shout It Out Loud” instead dangle from the rafters, floating down for hours. Stanley also contracted a bout of flu that forced the cancelation of three gigs in close proximity to the final show at Madison Square Garden.

Kiss had put decades into living up to their intro rap — “You wanted the best, you got the best” — but in the film they reveal how they faced long odds to make good on that claim in the lead-up to that MSG farewell show, which took place on Dec. 2, 2023. “These guys understood that for the film to be authentic, it had to be warts and all,” End of the Road’s director, DJ Viola, tells Rolling Stone via email. “Neither Gene nor Paul loved having a camera around during their lowest moments. Who would? But they understood why those moments mattered, and they trusted that the film would portray them honestly.”

Much of the documentary shows how hard Kiss work to get it right on the road, but longtime fans will be surprised to see how vulnerable their heroes appear. These are the guys who built their legend pouring their literal blood into the ink of a Marvel comic book, the guys whose hard-partying rock anthems influenced musicians as diverse as Nirvana, Pantera, and Garth Brooks. These are the guys who’ve plonked their logo on everything from condoms to caskets, the guys who kicked off a Farewell Tour in 2000 and refused to say goodbye. Related Content Kiss Take Their Curtain Call in New ‘End of the Road’ Doc Trailer At the 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame, Even Legends Had Notes on the Music Business Ace Frehley’s ‘Budokan’ Guitar, Kirk Hammett’s ‘Black Album’ Ouija Guitar Go to Auction Kiss’ Paul Stanley Touts New Avatar Spectacular in Vegas as More Interactive ‘Antithesis’ of the Sphere

Now Stanley is 74 and wants to spend time with his teenage kids, while Simmons is three years older and just wants to play gigs without Kiss’ heavy baggage — literally. “I’m a huge Radiohead fan,” Simmons says, “but if Thom [Yorke] got into my outfit, as my Italian friends in New York would say, fuhgeddaboudit.”  Of course, they made it to MSG, and the movie gives a front-row view to why Kiss have (finally) retired from touring.

“There certainly was a long period of time where we projected invincibility and immortality,” Stanley says. “I think to humanize that now doesn’t weaken who we are. It actually strengthens it. I’m a big believer that the less secrets you have, the more free you are.”

Simmons is more guarded about what ended up onscreen. “The doc is really an interesting exercise in trying to figure out what to show, what not to show,” he says. “All in all, I think it’s pretty good.”

“Neither Gene nor Paul asked me to remove a single moment from the film,” says Viola, who previously directed A&E’s Biography: KISStory. “There wasn’t one scene that made it in or was left out because of a note from either of them.”

THE FILM’S MOST REVEALING moments show Stanley and Simmons weighing the future of their career, and like a few great Kiss songs, one of the most telling scenes takes place in the backseat of a car:

Stanley: Look, we were just offered a lot to continue.Simmons: We were?Stanley: Yes.Simmons: I like money.Stanley: I like pride.

Ultimately, pride won out — at least regarding touring. Other than special engagements like the band’s “unmasked” performance at its own Kiss Kruise: Land Locked in Vegas event this past weekend, the duo swear Kiss are done on the road. But there’s still plenty of money to be made.

Even if Kiss, the band, are done, the idea of Kiss will continue. Simmons, ever playing the role of rock’s answer to Don King, hypes a future that could include a Kiss cartoon, theme park, biopic, and the avatar shows they teased at their final show. Their multimillion-dollar rights deal with Pophouse positions Kiss, the brand, well.

The business can keep going, but as the doc shows, Stanley and Simmons had to learn to let go of the stage itself. “At a certain point we decided, ‘OK, this is the top,'” Simmons says. “It’s not going to get any better.”

Since 2004, Stanley has had both hips replaced, both rotator cuffs repaired, and he’s undergone repair surgery for torn biceps. Most recently, he had shoulder surgery in 2021. He reckons Kiss played some 250 shows on the End of the Road tour while he was in his early 70s. “There are no 72-year-old football players, basketball players, or boxers,” he says. “I’ve sustained all the same injuries [as athletes]. …  On that final tour, that was our peak, to me, in terms of the band, the technology, the camaraderie.”

Stanley also feels good about bowing out now since Kiss have achieved what he calls “the trifecta”: trophies from the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame (they sit behind him on a marble table as he speaks), as well as a Kennedy Center Honor. Although Kiss redefined hard rock for multiple generations, their makeup and carnival stunts made them something of a pop-culture novelty to rock’s gatekeepers until recently. But good things come to those who wait, and Simmons and Stanley waited long enough.

“Kiss is timeless because Kiss has always been very adamant about not singing about politics or saving the whales or anything of that sort,” Stanley says. “There are people or media to take care of that. We’ve always been about, dare I say, great rock & roll, entertainment, escapism, and self-belief, preaching that if we can do this, you can do this.”

That raises an obvious question: Could accepting the Kennedy Center Honor, presented last year by President Trump, who plunged the Kennedy Center into turmoil, be perceived as political? “Not at all,” Simmons says. “Fuck politics. The Kennedy Center Honors are highest accolades a civilian can get … I don’t care how people think of the president. He was elected by the electoral college. … It’s fair. If you don’t like it, vote somebody else in. But in the meantime, he’s the president. And if you don’t like the person, at least respect the presidency.”

Putting aside politics, Simmons believes the End of the Road tour was “as good as we could do, and it’s never perfect.” Both musicians mention the glaring absence at the final show of the band’s other founding members, guitarist Ace Frehley (who later died in 2025) and drummer Peter Criss. “It became impossible, which shouldn’t be a surprise to me at this point,” Stanley says. “When people have either unrealistic expectations or demands, you just have to decide: Either you acquiesce or you move on.”

Simmons says he personally asked them multiple times to participate but they declined. “Paul may have said it better than I did,” he says, “which is, ‘We wouldn’t have been here without Ace and Peter, but Kiss wouldn’t have existed with Ace and Peter.’

“Even today, I love Peter to death,” he continues. “We went to the Kennedy Center Honors, and we were all sitting together and, it was great looking at old times. But Peter and his wife complained enough that the Secret Service just abandoned them and said, ‘OK. We’re done,’ and they just walked off. This is the Secret Service.” (A rep for Criss did not reply to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.)

One former Kiss member whom Simmons didn’t bother inviting to the final show was Vinnie Vincent, the reclusive guitarist who recently resurfaced hoping to sell CD singles for $225 and an entire album for $2 million. “He was a talented guy, but damaged, in my view,” Simmons says. “He has yet to this day to sign his contract with Kiss. …  I wish him well. I wish everybody well. Life is short, and if you can get $2,500 for popcorn farts or whatever it is you want to do, God bless.”

Largely, the duo has few regrets about how the tour turned out. “Everything turned out the way it was meant to,” Stanley says. His only “minuscule” regret is that the band was a little hasty in unveiling in-production sketches of the avatars that will be part of Kiss’ ABBA-like show. He promises the real deal will be so much better.

“We see sketches, and Paul and I get in there and try to massage it and ‘Kiss-ify’ it,” Simmons says. Then he paints a vivid picture of how he sees the avatar shows looking: “Imagine virtual reality glasses,” he says. “You walk into a room, you’re in another dimension or dinosaurs are about to eat you up, all kinds of stuff. Now imagine seeing that reality without wearing glasses.”

“I’ll get old, he won’t,” Stanley says of the avatar. “Again, Kiss should transcend its inception and continue for decades to come in different forms, whether it’s ‘Kiss meets Scooby-Doo’ or the End of the Road Tour or Kiss Kruises, whatever it is. I was going to say it’s part of Americana, but it’s worldwide. We created something far bigger than us.”

WHEN STANLEY WATCHES End of the Road, he says he’s impressed by what he calls “the magnitude” of it. “We’ve always had a sense of responsibility to our legacy and to what people expect from us,” he says. “This was really a commitment by us to make sure that people felt validated and justified in their love for us.”

“For the first time, you get to witness the dedication, work ethic, obsessiveness, and love that goes into every single performance,” Viola says. But he also sees it as something more: “What this documentary captures is the last time Kiss brought thousands of people together in an arena to share that experience as one collective. There’s something incredibly powerful about that.”

In the years leading up to the final tour, Stanley became aware of what he calls “flaws in the armor.” Kiss are hyperaware of those sorts of shortcomings and don’t want to let their fans down. That’s clear in the film’s scenes of meet-and-greets and a fun one showing Stanley rehearsing his “People, let me hear you” and “Make some noise” cheers to an empty stadium before the show. “That’s me,” he says, shouting those same words out loud over Zoom. “That’s not an act.”

Simmons is happy to be done with the physical burdens of playing in Kiss. “I’m 77 now,” he says. “I’m doing OK. I got lots of hair — unfortunately, more on my ass and my back — but you have to know when to stop doing the thing that limits you physically, because I literally cannot do the same things we did when we were in our twenties. Neither can Paul. It’s just life.” Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ John Mulaney Enlists Stepfather-in-Law's Country Band to Play 'Kimmel' The Lost Michael Jackson Tapes

Kiss have not broken up. Stanley describes Kiss’ next phase as “diversifying,” as they explore the upcoming avatar shows and what lies beyond. Simmons also says more music is on the way. “We actually secretly recorded a new song Paul wrote,” he says. “I can’t tell you more about it than that.”

“We’re not invincible, but [the idea of] Kiss is,” Stanley says. “Kiss is pretty much impervious to anything. But the people behind the band are human, ultimately — as much as we would like to think otherwise.”

#3271. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

The communications blackout offers a chance to learn things about handling errors autonomously and recording and storing data autonomously that should useful for other deep space missions. I wonder what the engineers are most worried about for that phase of the mission!

#3270. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

#3267. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3266. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the new update is shaping up to be pretty significant. In addition to expanding Siri AI support to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

macOS 27.3 also introduces Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, as well as native Live Activities support in the menu bar. Additionally, macOS 27.3 so far include native Markdown rendering in Quick Look, a new Pro Light screensaver, and additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links.
